newsitem.title: USA: U.S. hits back at China on human rights.
newsitem.headline: U.S. hits back at China on human rights.

text.p: The United States, replying to a broadside from Beijing, on Tuesday declared itself the world's human rights "champion" and said it does not appreciate being lectured by "authoritarian regimes" that are "major rights violators."

The comments came from State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns after Beijing hit back at U.S. accusations of China's human rights abuses, saying Washington was distorting facts while turning a blind eye to problems in its own back yard.

In a lengthy riposte to U.S. State Department criticism of China in its annual report on human rights, Beijing described the United States as a land of guns, terrorist bomb attacks and racial discrimination.

China's angry attack, carried by the official Xinhua news agency and titled: "A Look at the U.S. Human Rights Record," also said American-style political democracy was a game of the rich and faulted the U.S. Constitution for providing inadequate guarantees.

In response, Burns told reporters: "I don't think ... we need to listen to lectures from authoritarian countries about our human rights performance, because we are the world's champion of human rights."

Noting that the United States has always been a democracy, he suggested "the best way to understand that is that we have millions of people who want to come and live here (while) ...in most authoritarian countries around the world, you don't have millions of people trying to get in. You probably have millions of people trying to get out."
Burns acknowledged that the United States is "an imperfect country. We do have our own problems in this country. We have racial problems. We have problems of crime and terrorism."
But he said "we're very open about it" and "we're very proud of our human rights record here."
The U.S. report, released in January, accused Beijing of effectively silencing public dissent in 1996 through jailings, intimidation or exile.
China said the State Department was "once again distorting and attacking at length the state of human rights in China and more than 190 other countries and regions."
Burns said people around the world who have had their human rights taken away look to Washington to "speak up for them."

"And you know what? We're going to continue talking about human rights, because that's what Americans should do, given our history ... The message here ...is that we're very confident about our policy and emphasis on human rights. And we're not going to be deterred, especially by countries that are major violators of human rights," he added.

This is China's second lengthy rebuttal of its rights record since the latest State Department human rights report was made public in January. The rebuttals came before and after Secretary of State Madeleine Albright visited Beijing on Feb. 24 when Chinese officials went out of their way publicly to keep the atmosphere of the visit upbeat and positive.

The public Chinese defence comes as the United States and Europe are planning to co-sponsor a resolution criticising China's record at the U.N. Human Rights Commission meeting that begins in Geneva later this month.

Although Albright has said Washington is proceeding with the resolution, she has held out the possibility this could change if China made some gesture on human rights. But privately U.S. officials have said they do not expect anything sufficient from Beijing in the near term that would stave off the resolution moving forward.
